summary: Revaprazan is a potassium-competitive acid blocker (P-CAB) that reversibly inhibits the gastric H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) by competing with potassium, suppressing gastric acid secretion. It was developed and approved in South Korea (and used in some Asian markets) for acid-related conditions such as gastric and duodenal ulcer, gastritis, and reflux. Unlike conventional proton pump inhibitors it does not require acid activation, giving a more rapid onset and reversible binding. Revaprazan is NOT FDA-approved; this record is based on the Korean prescribing information and published literature rather than an FDA label.
indications: Treatment of gastritis (acute and chronic) with mucosal erosion
Acid-related dyspepsia / reflux symptoms (per regional approvals)

dosage.t: Once daily for up to 4 weeks
dosage.n: Per Korean labeling; individualise by response

dosage.t: Once daily for up to 8 weeks

admin: Take orally once daily, with or without food
Complete the prescribed course even if symptoms improve
Limit total duration to that approved for the indication
Avoid concurrent NSAIDs/aspirin where possible to support ulcer healing
moa: Revaprazan is a potassium-competitive acid blocker (P-CAB). It binds reversibly to the proton pump (H+/K+-ATPase) on gastric parietal cells at the potassium-binding site, competitively and reversibly inhibiting the final step of acid secretion. Because it does not require acid-mediated activation, it produces rapid and reversible acid suppression, distinct from the covalent, irreversible inhibition by conventional proton pump inhibitors.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to revaprazan or excipients
relative: Suspected gastric malignancy (acid suppression may mask symptoms)
monitor: Persistence of alarm symptoms suggestive of malignancy

preg: Safety in pregnancy has not been established and adequate human data are lacking. Avoid use during pregnancy unless the benefit clearly outweighs the unknown risk.
lact: It is not known whether revaprazan is excreted in human milk and safety during breastfeeding has not been established. Avoid use while breastfeeding.
renal: Data in renal impairment are limited. Use with caution; no well-established dose adjustment is defined.
hepatic: Revaprazan is metabolised in the liver (CYP3A4). Use with caution in hepatic impairment, with limited data; avoid in severe impairment. Monitor liver enzymes during prolonged use.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, clarithromycin) may increase revaprazan exposure; strong CYP3A4 inducers (rifampin) may reduce it
moderate: Drugs whose absorption is pH-dependent (e.g., ketoconazole, atazanavir, certain iron salts) may have altered absorption with raised gastric pH
Concomitant CYP3A4 substrates may be affected
minor: No clinically significant minor interactions established
interactions.food: May be taken regardless of food
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol, which irritates the gastric mucosa and may impair ulcer healing
interactions.diagnostics: Profound acid suppression may raise serum gastrin and can affect urea breath testing for H. pylori (false negatives) - hold before testing

rare: Effects of prolonged acid suppression (theoretical: enteric infection, malabsorption)

monitoring: Liver function tests with prolonged therapy
Alarm features (weight loss, bleeding, dysphagia) prompting endoscopy to exclude malignancy
counsel: Take the tablet once daily as prescribed and finish the full course
Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, severe abdominal pain, or persistent vomiting
Tell your doctor about all other medicines, since some need stomach acid to be absorbed
Avoid heavy alcohol and, where possible, painkillers like NSAIDs that can damage the stomach
Seek review if symptoms persist or you have warning signs such as weight loss or difficulty swallowing
pk: Rapid acid suppression (no acid activation required)
Plasma peak approximately 1-2 hours after oral dosing
Acid suppression sustained over the dosing interval with once-daily dosing
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture and light per the product label
pearls: Revaprazan is NOT FDA-approved - it was developed/approved in South Korea (Revanex) as one of the first P-CABs; this record is based on the Korean prescribing information and literature, not an FDA label
As a P-CAB it reversibly and competitively blocks the proton pump without needing acid activation, giving faster onset than conventional PPIs
Profound acid suppression can cause false-negative urea breath/stool antigen tests for H. pylori - hold before testing
Newer P-CABs such as vonoprazan have largely superseded revaprazan in clinical use
Exclude gastric malignancy in patients with alarm features before attributing symptoms to benign acid-related disease
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is nearly time for the next dose, skip the missed one and continue your usual once-daily schedule. Do not double the dose.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited. Expect exaggerated acid-suppressant effects and possible gastrointestinal symptoms or dizziness. There is no specific antidote; manage supportively with symptom-directed care and observation. Revaprazan is protein-bound, so dialysis is unlikely to be effective.
